hello.note: All-purpose greeting for any time of day or status, unlike the ina kwana time-of-day exchange below; also doubles as a gentle 'sorry to hear that' when someone looks tired or has had trouble.

good_morning.note: Literally 'how was the night'; the standard morning greeting, answered Lafiya lau (all is well). Barka da safiya is a more literal 'good morning' alternative.

good_evening.note: The direct, dictionary 'good evening' (also covers afternoon); Ina wuni? (how has the day been) is a related midday check-in but isn't itself an evening greeting, so it's dropped here in favor of the literal, widely attested form.

goodbye.note: Literally 'until it's been a while'; the everyday way to say see you later.

how_are_you.note: Addressed to a man; ask a woman Yaya kike? Casual either way, and both are answered Lafiya lau.

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'it's nothing'; the standard reply to Na gode. Marabanku/Barka da zuwa (welcoming an arriving guest) is a false friend here: it answers a different sense of English 'welcome' and is barely used as a reply to thanks.

no_problem.note: Literally 'not a problem'; a distinct, well-attested reassurance from Ba komai above, used e.g. after a favor or small apology.

please.note: Literally 'for God's sake'; the ordinary everyday word for please, not felt as especially religious.

excuse_me.note: Pardon-me for getting someone's attention or passing by; real usage shows Yi hakuri/Ku yi hakuri lean toward apologizing or asking for patience over a fault, not this polite interruption, so Gafara (often softened to Gafara dai) is the better match.

of_course.note: Literally 'certainly'; I mana is a common casual alternative.

cheers.note: Literally 'health'; Hausa has no single dedicated toast word, and speakers often just say Cheers in English or use this as a health wish over tea or kola nut.
